newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Giscard opens Pandora's box on franc.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Giscard opens Pandora's box on franc.

text.p: France and Germany moved swiftly on Thursday to stamp out fears of a franc crisis after former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called for a depreciation of the French currency.

The ex-president's comments had touched a raw nerve, not just about the franc but about the whole drive to European monetary union amid fears that persistent mass unemployment would turn out to be the price of a single currency.
In a joint statement issued in Paris and Bonn, French Prime Minister Alain Juppe and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl reaffirmed their commitment to launch the single currency on schedule in 1999.

They also said they agreed in a telephone conversation on Thursday afternoon that the franc-mark rate was in line with fundamentals. But despite that the French currency fell to a two-month low against the mark in Europe.

In Bonn, Giscard d'Estaing, who called in an article in weekly l'Express for a sharp depreciation in the franc to revive growth and employment, stressed the main object of his comments was the dollar rather than the mark.
On Wednesday, however, he acknowledged his call for a stronger dollar implied a fall in the franc against the mark.

He also attacked a decade-old policy of pegging the French currency to the mark, despite the sharp rise in German interest rates after unification in 1990 which pushed up the mark and dragged up other satellite European currencies with it.
Although the ex-president wields little political clout, he was one of the first high-ranking politicians in recent years to break publicly a taboo on questioning the strong franc policy.
Traditional opponents of European monetary union were quick to jump on the bandwagon started by someone who has been long associated with the construction of Europe.

"Valery Giscard d'Estaing has hit the nail on the head by stating that employment is the absolute priority," Gaullist National Assembly speaker and former anti-Maastricht campaigner Philippe Seguin said on Thursday.
Giscard d'Estaing had finally seen sense, right-wing Eurosceptic Philippe de Villiers said. Europeans were prisoners in an overvalued currency zone and needed change to revive growth and jobs.

Former interior minister Charles Pasqua issued a statement saying that more and more French people were questioning a policy designed purely to meet the single currency goal at the expense of the economy, investment and jobs.

Economists said the comments by Seguin in particular had helped drive down the franc, already under pressure on Wednesday, to a two-month low of 3.3924 per mark on Thursday compared with 3.3797 late on Tuesday.

Giscard d'Estaing's comments were well timed to strike a chord in a country where people are increasingly willing to blame record 12.6 percent unemployment on government policies and the drive to monetary union.

Opinion polls show Prime Minister Alain Juppe is the most unpopular since the Fifth Republic was founded in 1958. His office has been forced to deny repeated rumours first he might quit, and more recently, that he would reshuffle his government.
At the same time, even European visionaries like former European Commission President Jacques Delors have expressed reservations recently about the direction in which Europe is heading.
If France voted today, it would not back the Maastricht Treaty, he said last month.
